Key Takeaways

CISA AA26-194A provides actionable guidance to improve the security of Internet-facing Cisco routers against real-world attack techniques.

The advisory focuses on configuration hardening and security hygiene, rather than a single vulnerability or CVE.

Manually validating advisory recommendations across enterprise networks is difficult, time-consuming, and prone to inconsistencies.

Qualys Policy Audit transforms advisory guidance into automated configuration compliance checks, enabling organizations to continuously assess Cisco router configurations.

Organizations can quickly identify configuration gaps, prioritize remediation, and continuously measure compliance using an out-of-the-box assessment policy.

Cybersecurity advisories provide valuable guidance for defending against evolving threats, but their true value lies in how quickly organizations can translate recommendations into measurable security controls. With the release of the CISA Joint Cybersecurity Advisory AA26-194A, security teams now have concrete guidance to strengthen the security posture of their Internet-facing Cisco routers. With Qualys Policy Audit, organizations can automate configuration assessments to operationalize these crucial recommendations.

It is crucial to acknowledge that actors sponsored by the Russian state are actively exploiting misconfigured and vulnerable networking devices, such as Cisco routers, to penetrate enterprise and critical infrastructure networks. This access enables them to move deeper into these environments without detection. In response, CISA, the NSA, and international partners have published AA26-194A, which provides clear guidance on hardening these devices against these threats.

Organizations must understand that the guidance isn’t the hard part; the real challenge lies in ensuring that every router in production adheres to it. This is the gap where most organizations struggle. Addressing that gap requires ongoing compliance verification rather than a one-time assessment. It is important to start assessing your Cisco routers in accordance with the advisory’s recommendations.

Understanding CISA AA26-194A

CISA is committed to enhancing cybersecurity and regularly publishes periodically Joint Cybersecurity Advisories in collaboration with the National Security Agency (NSA) and other international partners. AA26-194A, titled Improve Router Hygiene to Protect Against Russian State-Sponsored Targeting, delivers crucial insights based on real-world threat intelligence, incident response findings, and observed attacker techniques.

This advisory shows that attackers exploit weak configurations, legacy management protocols, insecure administrative access, and unsupported devices to infiltrate enterprise networks.

It is crucial to implement the advisory’s recommendations, which focus on fundamental security practices. These include using the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), restricting management access, disabling unnecessary services, removing insecure default configurations, maintaining updated software versions, and continuously monitoring network device configurations. Taking these steps is essential for ensuring robust network security and resilience against potential threats.

Routers are the frontline defense systems exposed to the internet, making them crucial in safeguarding enterprise networks. A single insecure configuration can enable attackers to establish persistence, intercept traffic, or move laterally within the environment.

Even organizations with mature vulnerability management programs often overlook configuration weaknesses, which attackers frequently exploit. The recommendations in AA26-194A help close this configuration gap by guiding organizations toward secure practices that strengthen the security posture of their Cisco network devices.

For organizations managing hundreds or thousands of Cisco devices, manually reviewing configurations is impractical, and a lack of visibility can slow remediation. Addressing it should be a priority.

The Operational Challenge

Understanding a security advisory may seem straightforward, but assessing whether hundreds or even thousands of network devices comply with that guidance is a formidable challenge. Many security teams are stuck relying on manual Command-Line Interface (CLI) reviews, spreadsheets, or custom scripts, which not only consume valuable time but also increase the likelihood of inconsistent assessments and make ongoing compliance monitoring difficult to sustain. Organizations need a robust solution that turns advisory recommendations into continuous, repeatable, and measurable compliance checks.

Transforming Guidance into Continuous Compliance

Qualys Policy Audit decisively addresses the challenges organizations face with AA26-194A by providing an out-of-the-box policy that automates the assessment of Cisco router configurations against the advisory’s recommended security practices. Built on the core principle of continuous visibility into every control, this platform harnesses AI-powered risk-based prioritization, ensures automated remediation with audit-ready evidence by default, and strengthens identity and access governance to eliminate ownership gaps, all while mapping compliance across more than 100 frameworks.

Instead of engaging in painstaking manual reviews of each configuration, security teams receive a real-time of their Cisco network infrastructure. Non-compliant devices are swiftly identified automatically, and remediation efforts areprioritized based on actionable compliance results.

The policy rigorously automates the validation of critical security recommendations from the advisory, including secure SNMP configuration, hardened management services and remote administration, stronger password and authentication controls, restricted management access, software lifecycle and support validation, and essential additional hardening practices for Cisco routers.

Benefits of Automated Assessment

With Qualys Policy Audit, organizations can:

Assess Cisco router configurations against CISA guidance on a recurring schedule.

Identify insecure configurations before attackers can exploit them.

Reduce the manual effort needed to respond to newly published advisories.

Prioritize remediation by risk, so resources go where they matter most.

Demonstrate alignment with recommended security practices through audit-ready compliance reporting.

Detect configuration drift between assessments rather than relying on a one-time check.

Qualys states that Policy Audit can cut manual compliance tasks by up to 90% through automated evidence collection and reporting.

Conclusion

Cybersecurity advisories offer critical security guidance, but relying solely on guidance will not enhance security. Organizations must actively measure, validate, and continuously monitor the implementation of these recommendations to ensure effectiveness.

With the out-of-the-box CISA AA26-194A policy in Qualys Policy Audit, security teams can automate Cisco router configuration assessments. This enables them to swiftly identify configuration weaknesses and significantly strengthen their network security posture through ongoing compliance monitoring.

As organizations face increasingly complex network environments, automating configuration assessments is not just beneficial but essential for turning security guidance into measurable, repeatable security outcomes.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

What is CISA AA26-194A?

A joint cybersecurity advisory published July 13, 2026, titled Improve Router Hygiene to Protect Against Russian State-Sponsored Targeting. It describes FSB Center 16’s exploitation of poorly configured networking devices and lists hardening steps.

Is this about a single CVE?

No. The primary path is configuration hygiene, especially SNMP and management access. Actors also use Cisco Smart Install and known CVEs such as CVE-2018-0171 and CVE-2008-4128.

What does the Qualys policy check?

Cisco router configurations against the advisory’s recommended practices: SNMP, management services, password and authentication controls, restricted management access, software lifecycle, and additional hardening.

Does Policy Audit replace the advisory?

No. It operationalizes the technical configuration recommendations so teams can assess them continuously. Network design, monitoring, and incident response stay with the organization.

What should I do first?

Disable Cisco Smart Install, move to SNMPv3 with authPriv, restrict management protocols to an out-of-band network, and confirm unsupported devices are scheduled for replacement. Then use continuous assessment so the check does not stop at the first review.

Title: Waiting on a Node.js Upgrade? Build a Stopgap with the Controls You Own
Context: In the meantime, interim mitigations from the Qualys Threat Research Unit narrow the Brotli, DNS, TLS, and keep-alive attack paths, and WAF, IPS, and EDR protections from major...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Node.js has fixed CVE-2026-111497, a Brotli decoder flaw that can permit remote code execution, in 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, but upgrading at scale is slow. In Qualys telemetry, only 42,000 of roughly 3 million Node.js installations have been patched, and 1.7 million run end-of-life lines that will never receive a fix. In the meantime, interim mitigations from the Qualys Threat Research Unit narrow the Brotli, DNS, TLS, and keep-alive attack paths, and WAF, IPS, and EDR protections from major vendors add further layers. Soon, Qualys ETM will factor these controls into risk scores. These controls buy time, but upgrading the runtime remains the only complete fix.

Node.js comes with a clear instruction: upgrade the runtime. The October 21 security release fixes 10 vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-111497, a Brotli decoder flaw that can permit remote code execution, and three high-severity flaws that weaken DNS and TLS hostname validation. Fixed releases exist for the 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x lines. Upgrading at this scale still takes time, because the vulnerable code lives in the runtime itself, in container images, single-executable applications, and serverless functions that dependency checks never touch. In Qualys telemetry, only 42,000 of the 3.3 million installations have been patched so far, and 1.7 million run end-of-life versions, including 25.x, 23.x, 21.x, and 20.x, that will not receive a fix and must move to a supported line.

Those first days are where mitigations and compensating controls earn their place. They reduce risk while upgrades roll out, and the right visibility shows which runtimes need attention first. Our Node.js blog post covers vulnerabilities, fixed versions, and detection methods.

Here is how to bridge the gap between disclosure and upgrade, in four steps: find and prioritize exposed Node.js, apply interim mitigations, layer the controls you already run, then patch and verify.

Step 1: Find and Prioritize Exposed Node.js

Qualys customers can search for assets affected by CVE-2026-111497 and the other October 2026 Node.js CVEs to see every Node.js runtime across hosts, containers, and cloud workloads. That includes copies that dependency checks miss, such as those in version managers, application folders, and bundled runtimes.

It is important to note that not every vulnerable runtime has the same level of exposure. Start with internet-facing services that decompress untrusted Brotli data (CVE-2026-111497), since they are the most direct path to remote code execution. Services that open TLS connections to user-supplied hosts (CVE-2026-106069, CVE-2026-105483) come next. Runtimes on end-of-life lines need an upgrade plan, as no patches will be available for them. Consider these factors alongside business criticality to decide what to mitigate and upgrade first.

Step 2: Apply Interim Mitigations

Node.js has no official workaround, but the Qualys Threat Research Unit has identified practical interim steps. Each one narrows a specific attack path while you plan the upgrade, and together they complement the fix.

These changes do not eliminate all exploitation paths associated with these CVEs, and some changes may affect application behavior. Therefore, it is crucial to test the affected applications after each change.

Limit Brotli exposure (CVE-2026-111497). Avoid decompressing Brotli from untrusted sources where you can, and cap payload size and decompression ratio at the reverse proxy or WAF.

Use the safer DNS call (CVE-2026-105482). Resolve user-supplied names with dns.lookup instead of dns.resolve*, and reject hostnames that contain NUL characters.

Canonicalize IP addresses (CVE-2026-106069, CVE-2026-105483, CVE-2026-106072). Convert addresses to canonical form before they reach a TLS connection, and reject fullwidth and other non-canonical forms.

Turn off keep-alive for untrusted servers (CVE-2026-105481). Disable keepAlive on http.Agent for connections to servers you do not control.

Treat the Permission Model as advisory. (CVE-2026-106071, CVE-2026-106073) Do not rely on it as a security boundary on affected versions.

Step 3: Add Layers from the Security Stack You Already Run

The tools already in your environment can work alongside the interim steps, each at a different point in the attack path. Each layer can catch what the one before it misses.

Edge and network: WAF and IPS. WAF and IPS vendors such as Cloudflare, Fortinet, and Check Point have released protections that name the Brotli flaw. They help block exploit requests before those requests reach the Node.js decoder.

After exploitation: EDR. Behavioral and exploit-prevention policies in endpoint tools such as CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, and Cortex XDR add a second line of defense. They help stop what an attacker tries next, such as a Node.js process spawning a shell or downloading a binary, and some also act on the memory exploitation itself.

Step 4: Patch, Restart, and Re-Validate

Interim mitigations reduce risk. Upgrading remains the only complete fix. Node.js fixed these flaws in 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, while lines such as 25.x, 23.x, 21.x, 20.x, and older receive no fix and must move to a supported release. Customers can deploy supported vendor patches through TruRisk Eliminate, so check the patch catalog for their line. Qualys reports a high patch reliability rating for these updates and no OS reboot requirement for the runtime upgrade.

Confirm That Remediation Is Complete

A patch isn’t finished when the package installs:

Upgrade every copy. Migrate end-of-life lines to a supported release.

Rebuild container images and single-executable applications on the fixed version, then redeploy them.

Restart every service that runs on Node.js. Long-running processes, containers, and single-executable applications keep the vulnerable runtime in memory until they restart.

Rescan and verify. Rescan with Cloud Agent or Container Security and confirm the detection QIDs are closed.

Where to Start

Find. Search for CVE-2026-111497 and the other October 2026 Node.js CVEs to locate every runtime, including copies outside standard install paths.

Prioritize. Put internet-facing services that decompress untrusted Brotli data at the top, alongside business criticality.

Mitigate. Apply the Qualys TRU interim steps to runtimes awaiting an upgrade, and test the affected applications.

Layer. Keep applicable WAF, IPS, and EDR protections enabled and current as additional layers, and set the Cloudflare rule to Block.

Patch and verify. Upgrade to a fixed release, rebuild and redeploy what embeds the runtime, restart every Node.js service, and rescan.

Compensating controls buy valuable time, but they do not remove the flaw. Keep tracking every system until it is patched.

Coming Next: Give Your Controls Credit in Qualys ETM

The capabilities described in this section are in development and subject to change.

Two servers can run the same unpatched Node.js build and carry very different risks. One sits behind a WAF rule and an IPS signature that name the Brotli flaw, with EDR watching its Node.js process. The other faces the internet with nothing in front of it. A traditional scan reports them the same way.

Qualys ETM is being extended to close that gap. It arrives in three steps:

Controls reflected in the score. Controls that are in place will lower a finding’s QVSS score to reflect your actual defenses, shown as the Environmental score, so remediation queues focus on what still needs attention.

Title: How to Identify Compromised eMudhra Certificates With Qualys (CVE-2026-111943)
Context: Exploitation: eMudhra says only one of the affected intermediates was used in production, and none of them issued certificates to websites or end users
Full Text:
Executive Summary

A critical certificate authority incident disclosed on October 17, 2026, impacts eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates. A flaw in the key generation process could allow attackers to recover private keys and issue fraudulent TLS or code-signing certificates. The affected intermediates have been revoked and blocked by major platform vendors, including Chrome, Mozilla, Apple, and Microsoft. The issue is tracked as CVE-2026-111943.

The eMudhra Certificate Authority Compromise

On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported recovering the private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates after discovering that the underlying cryptographic keys contained only a fraction of the expected entropy. Browser and OS vendors have since blocked the certificates, and eMudhra has revoked them. Security teams now face an immediate question: Where do certificates issued by the compromised eMudhra intermediates exist within my environment?

Qualys VMDR and Qualys Certificate View already collect the data needed to answer that. This post explains how to use them, with QQL queries you can run today.

What is eMudhra?

eMudhra, a digital trust and cybersecurity provider, offers solutions spanning Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), digital certificates, identity management, and secure digital transactions. Recent security concerns involving eight of its intermediate Certificate Authority (CA) certificates highlight the importance of strong cryptographic key generation, rigorous validation, and continuous oversight of digital trust infrastructure. The incident reinforces a critical security lesson: trust in digital certificates depends not just on the technology, but on the operational controls protecting the keys behind them.

What Happened

A flaw in eMudhra’s key generation process produced a second set of weak P-384 keys during a wrap/unwrap step, and those weak keys were mistakenly used for eight intermediate CA certificates. This flaw reduced the effective entropy of the affected P-384 keys to an estimated 3 to 8 bits, making private-key recovery trivial to compute.

The weak keys came from a key generation ceremony held on April 30, 2025, for 24 subordinate CAs. Anyone holding the private key of one of these intermediates could issue a certificate that impersonates any website or service, subject to each client’s validation controls. Some key points about the incident:

Six of the eight intermediates are TLS CAs; two are code-signing CAs.

Browsers: Chrome, Mozilla, and Apple have blocked the TLS certificates, and Microsoft has blocked the two code-signing certificates.

Root distrust: Google removed the emSign ECC Root CA – G3 from the Chrome Root Store, and Mozilla removed trust in the root that signed the intermediates.

eMudhra: has revoked the eight certificates and stopped issuing new certificates under its G3 root. It states that its root CA private keys and other intermediate CAs are not affected, and that the issue is limited to its global website-security business, not Indian DSC and eSign services.

Exploitation: eMudhra says only one of the affected intermediates was used in production, and none of them issued certificates to websites or end users.

Who is at Most Risk?

Organizations should prioritize investigation if they:

Operate internet-facing websites, APIs, VPNs, or other TLS-enabled services.

Use publicly trusted certificates issued through eMudhra or emSign trust hierarchies.

Distribute signed software that relies on publicly trusted code-signing certificates.

Develop or run applications built on the Go programming language.

Maintain legacy systems, unmanaged endpoints, or custom trust stores that may not receive certificate distrust updates automatically.

How Can Qualys VMDR and Certificate View Help Identify eMudhra Certificates?

Use Certificate View, included with VMDR, to identify certificates issued by affected eMudhra authorities and use VMDR with Cloud Agent to identify hosts running vulnerable Go installations or software requiring vendor-issued updates.

Step 1: Make Sure Coverage Is Complete

Entitle Certificate View on your VMDR scan ranges. Confirm that the IP ranges you scan with VMDR are enabled in Certificate View.

Add external domains. For sites hosted by web or app providers, add the FQDNs or IP addresses in Certificate View. It runs a lightweight scan across standard ports to detect TLS services and analyze their certificates.

Use Cloud Agent where scans cannot reach. Agents report software and certificate data from endpoints, servers, and remote workers that network scans miss.

Step 2: Pinpoint the Eight Compromised Intermediates

To confirm whether any of the eight compromised intermediates appear in a chain, search for their SHA-256 fingerprints, serial numbers, or issuer names in Certificate View > Certificates.

Reference QQL Queries

By Issuer:

certificate:(issuer.name:[`EM EV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM OV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM DV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM EV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM OV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM DV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM OV CS CA – G3B`, `EM OV CS CA – G3C`])

By Serial Number:

certificate:(serialNumber:`c7c41efe92d825f05eae841a4a82c1` or serialNumber:`6cada367fb1c100088120ea202d568` or serialNumber:`a4aee678f23362b4c0e460b772f214` or serialNumber:`8009928a64107601af05fa2f19f109` or serialNumber:`296926c227a3a1526392b19482a504` or serialNumber:`588b2e3c2bb8cda13e1a1209254321` or serialNumber:`7818933f8f85b4619a2b35fba83d0a` or serialNumber:`544b7f922c31ae220a4a922916f6e6`)

The Information tab shows the fingerprints, serial number, and first and last found dates so that you can compare them with the SHA-256 values in the table.

Step 3: Find Software That Still Trusts the Affected Certificates

Certificates presented by your servers are only half of the exposure. Applications running older Go runtimes may continue to trust certificate chains containing the compromised intermediates. VMDR/Cloud Agent can help you find them.

Find Go toolchains to update

Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 block certificate chains that contain any of the eight compromised keys (CVE-2026-111943). Qualys has released QID 5019897 for SwCA scanning to detect affected Go versions. Before you scan, confirm your agents have the latest signatures that include this QID, so the new scan picks it up. Then open the Vulnerabilities tab and use the query below to list the impacted assets:

In addition to software detection, Qualys is releasing QID 48395: eMudhra Intermediate CA Certificates Enumeration. Optional Check: Find eMudhra-Issued Certificates with QQL Queries in Certificate View

Open Certificate View > Certificates, paste the query below into the search bar, and run it. It matches any certificate whose issuer organization is one of the eMudhra entities in the affected list.

certificate:(issuer.organization:`eMudhra BV` or issuer.organization:`eMudhra Inc`)

The results list each certificate with its issuer, validity dates, and the assets and ports where it was found. Use the left-pane filters, such as Expiring Certificates and Certificate Authority, to sort the results by urgency.

The two organizations that matter most for this incident are eMudhra BV and eMudhra Inc, because they are the organizations named on the eight compromised intermediates (the G3B and G3C certificates).

Tip: save the query as a dashboard widget in Certificate View, so any new eMudhra-issued certificate that appears is flagged automatically.

Response and Remediation

Replace affected certificates first. Any leaf certificate whose chain includes one of the eight intermediates should be reissued by another trusted CA and redeployed with the correct chain.

Updates. Apply operating system security updates and upgrade Go runtimes to supported releases that reject certificate chains containing the compromised intermediates.

Confirm revocation behavior. eMudhra has revoked the eight certificates, but clients that do not check revocation can still accept them. Validate that certificate revocation checks are functioning correctly and that revocation lists are up to date.

Monitor continuously. Monitor dashboards after each scan cycle until results are clean.

The eMudhra incident is a reminder that trust depends on both the certificates you present and the authorities you trust. Title: The Science of Exploitability: Decoding BlueHammer
Context: Exploitation depends on a reachable vulnerable path, the privileges an attacker starts with, the available services and components, and the system’s current state
Full Text:
Executive Summary

BlueHammer (CVE-2026-33825) is an eight-stage local privilege-escalation chain targeting the Windows Defender Antimalware Platform before 4.18.26030.3011. It does not grant initial access; an attacker needs standard-user code execution first. Still, in the lab, it reached NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, recovered domain-admin credentials from LSASS, and moved laterally via pass-the-hash. This is not memory corruption. It chains CloudFilter callbacks, batch oplocks, object-manager symlinks, Defender’s update RPC, offline SAM parsing, and SAMR. Crucially, affected is not the same as exploitable: runtime factors — pending signature update, WinDefend state, filter drivers, VSS, CloudFilter reachability decide whether the path works on a given host. That’s the gap version-based scanning can’t close. Qualys TruConfirm marks a host Exploit Validated only after environmental checks, plus a non-destructive BAS validation of the CloudFilter freeze (Stages 2–3), no SAM extraction, no password reset, no service creation, no SYSTEM shell.

Introduction and Execution Flow

A CVE tells you what could go wrong. It does not tell you whether an attacker can actually make it happen on your machine. Exploitation depends on a reachable vulnerable path, the privileges an attacker starts with, the available services and components, and the system’s current state. Exploitability analysis brings these signals together to answer a practical question: can this vulnerability be exploited on this machine right now?

BlueHammer provides a concrete case study. Windows Defender is an always-running, highly privileged component whose filter drivers, RPC interfaces, scanning engine, and update mechanisms operate with SYSTEM authority. Publicly tracked as CVE-2026-33825, BlueHammer combines these trusted components in an eight-stage local privilege-escalation chain. Microsoft identifies Defender Antimalware Platform versions earlier than 4.18.26030.3011 as affected; our reverse-engineering host ran version 4.18.2104.10.

BlueHammer does not provide initial access. An attacker must first obtain code execution as a standard user, potentially through phishing, malicious content, or abuse of valid accounts. In our lab, the exploit abused Defender’s privileged update and file-handling paths to obtain NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. From that shell, we recovered credential material for CITRIX\administrator that was already present in LSASS. Using pass-the-hash, we authenticated to the domain controller as CITRIX\administrator, and then accessed protected system locations, started services, and extracted NTDS.dit. This demonstrated the tested path from a user-level foothold to verified domain-administrator control.

The complete tested attack path, along with its potential follow-on impact, is as follows:

Initial Access → BlueHammer Execution → Local SYSTEM → LSASS Credential Access → Pass-the-Hash → Domain Controller Access as CITRIX\administrator → Domain Compromise → Potential Follow-on Activity (not performed)

BlueHammer does not depend on memory corruption. Instead, it integrates several components, including cloud files, callbacks, opportunistic locks, object-manager symbolic links, Defender’s local update RPC interface, offline registry parsing, and SAMR operations, with each stage preparing the next. We reconstructed the chain by reverse-engineering the original FunnyApp.exe binary in IDA Pro and tracing it in x64dbg. The subsequent sections explain the eight stages, the verified post-exploitation path, and how Qualys TruConfirm safely validates vulnerable customer environments before an attacker reaches the destructive stages.

Test environment used for this analysis:

PoC binary: FunnyApp.exe (SHA-256 : f4ffef4204880031a6a532ff5c1b5686e6a301c365f492071c1d462fa5b6b4a0)

Host: DESKTOP38, Windows 11 Pro 21H2, OS build 22000.2295

Defender platform: 4.18.2104.10 | Engine: 1.1.17300.4 | Security intelligence: 1.321.69.0

Real-time protection: enabled

This article discusses two distinct test contexts. Reverse engineering and end-to-end debugging were performed on DESKTOP38 using the original, unmodified FunnyApp.exe PoC whose SHA-256 is listed above. The TruConfirm’s evidence presented later was collected from the validation asset BlackHat2-CVE-2026-33825, which utilized a modified, non-destructive PoC. This validation process stops before any actions such as: SAM extraction, password modification, service creation, credential recovery, or shell execution.

Figure 1: BlueHammer’s eight-stage execution flow, from Windows Update precheck to interactive SYSTEM shell.

Exploit Reasoning

BlueHammer’s approach to determining exploitability is tailored to each host. While identifying an affected version of Defender indicates a vulnerability, it does not guarantee that the vulnerable path is reachable or that the complete exploit chain can execute successfully. The effectiveness of the exploit is influenced by runtime and environmental factors, which may vary across similar endpoints.

The analysis begins by considering the attacker’s perspective, especially their ability to execute code as a standard user. Several critical factors are assessed, including the Defender platform version, the status of WinDefend and its real-time protection, the presence of necessary filter drivers, the availability of Volume Shadow Copy, and the existence of pending updates to Defender signatures. It also checks whether the CloudFilter and Defender update paths are reachable based on the current privilege level.

In the case assessed, the Defender platform version 4.18.2104.10 was found to meet all required conditions. The original PoC demonstrated that it completed all eight stages of the exploit, gaining a SYSTEM shell, recovering domain-administrator credentials from LSASS, and authenticating to the domain controller via pass-the-hash. This confirmed not only that the host was running an affected version but also that the entire exploit process worked correctly within its actual configuration and system state.

On the other hand, TruConfirm adopts a proactive strategy in customer environments. It initiates the process by verifying that all required environmental factors are in place. Following this, it employs a modified Qualys Breach and Attack Simulation workflow to replicate only the non-destructive aspects of the exploit. This step is crucial for confirming the accessibility of the critical CloudFilter primitive. The validation process focuses on the relevant behaviors from Stages 2 and 3, ensuring the Defender freeze and a clean Defender release. It does not perform potentially harmful actions such as extracting SAM data, resetting passwords, creating a service, recovering credentials, obtaining a SYSTEM shell, or reproducing the domain-compromise path demonstrated in the original PoC. An endpoint is designated as “Exploit Validated” only when it successfully passes environmental checks and validation. This thorough approach yields stronger, host-specific evidence than relying solely on version detection, all while avoiding the execution of destructive and post-exploitation phases of the original PoC.

Stage 0 — Windows Update Precheck

The exploit begins by querying the standard Microsoft.Update.Session COM interface to determine whether a Defender signature update is pending. It specifically filters Windows Update (WU) results by the category ID E0789628-CE08-4437-BE74-2495B842F43B, which is associated with Definition Updates. This GUID serves as a distinctive identifier within the .rdata section, effectively acting as a hunting signature. If no updates are pending, the exploit will terminate without further action. For the subsequent stages to successfully hijack the update consumption process, a pending update is crucial. Additionally, this initial check serves as a soft-target filter, since systems on aggressive update schedules typically do not retain pending updates long enough for the exploit to be operational.

Stage 1 — Signed Package Download and CAB Extraction

The exploit begins by downloading Microsoft’s signed executable file, mpam-fex64.exe, from fwlink and extracting its embedded CAB payload without saving it to disk. It mimics a Chrome/141.0.0.0 User-Agent in the HTTPS request, which is atypical for a native binary, and reads the response into a buffer via InternetReadFile. Then, GetCabFileFromBuff extracts the CAB payload from the executable by locating its header and creates custom I/O callbacks to handle the file. This results in the extraction of five files: mpasbase: vdm, mpavdlta.vdm, and mpengine.dll. In the exploit, specifically, it replaces the mpasbase.vdm file with a malicious version, while keeping the other four stay byte-identical to the legitimate signed originals. This tactic helps the exploit evade detection by allowing Windows Defender’s update-engine signature checks to pass successfully.

Figure 2: Stage 1 — fwlink download of mpam-fex64.exe and in-memory CAB extraction.

Stage 2 — Oplock Signaling on RstrtMgr.dll

The exploit relies on precise timing to detect when Defender begins scanning a file it has placed on the system. Since there is no official API to achieve this, the exploit cleverly combines two documented methods. It initiates a batch oplock on RstrtMgr.dll, a system DLL frequently accessed during Defender’s scanning process, and subsequently creates an EICAR test file to trigger a scan.

To implement this, the exploit first writes the EICAR file and opens RstrtMgr.dll with the FILE_FLAG_OVERLAPPED flag. It then requests a batch oplock via a DeviceIoControl call with control code 0x90008. Opening the EICAR file initiates Defender’s real-time scanning. The exploit then uses GetOverlappedResult to wait for Defender’s scanning process to touch RstrtMgr.dll and release the oplock, signaling the start of the scan. In the background, a thread named ShadowCopyFinderThread monitors the NT object namespace for any VSS snapshots that Defender may create during its scans. As Defender often uses shadow copies, the exploit captures its path for later use. In the context of an exploit, when a specific condition arises, the exploit captures the path of the VSS copy, typically designated at \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopyN. This captured path is then stored for later use in Stage 6 of the exploit. During this stage, the exploit manipulates the process by redirecting Windows Defender’s file access to the system’s Security Account Manager (SAM) file, located at \??\<fullvsspath>\Windows\System32\Config\SAM on the previously captured shadow copy.

To evade detection, the EICAR string is stored in reverse within the binary’s .rdata section and is reversed again at runtime, ensuring the binary does not trigger Defender’s EICAR signature detection. Notably, the 0x90008 FSCTL code, used to establish the oplock, reappears in later stages of the exploit, indicating a strong signal: two independent batch oplocks are present in a single binary.

Figure 3: Stage 2 — TriggerWDForVS: EICAR drop, RstrtMgr.dll oplock, wait for Defender scan.

Stage 3 — Freezing MsMpEng.exe via the CloudFilter Callback

The Stage 3 exploit targets Windows Defender’s scanning engine, MsMpEng.exe, by placing it in a controlled wait state. This manipulation allows the exploit to perform file operations without interference from Defender. The technique leverages the behavior of the Cloud Files subsystem, particularly the CloudFilter minifilter (cldflt.sys), which intentionally blocks a thread in kernel mode while awaiting completion from a user-mode synchronization provider. The intentional wait in the process allows cloud providers, such as OneDrive, to perform network I/O operations necessary to retrieve and prepare a file before delivering its data to the requester. It’s important to note that there is no predefined limit to the duration of this wait.

To implement this strategy, the exploit registers itself as a CloudFilter provider for a sync-root directory it controls and drops a decoy executable named foo.exe in that directory. When the real-time scanner of MsMpEng detects the executable file foo.exe, which is prioritized for scanning by Defender, the driver cldflt.sys activates a callback to fetch placeholders within the process associated with the exploit. At this point, the exploit checks whether the caller’s process ID, CF_PROCESS_INFO, matches the WinDefend service’s process ID obtained via QueryServiceStatusEx. If they match, the callback halts the operation using an event controlled by the exploit’s worker thread. This effectively keeps MsMpEng stalled in the waiting state of cldflt.sys, enabling the exploit to proceed without detection by Windows Defender.

Figure 4: Stage 3 — the \foo.exe decoy filename hard-coded as a wide-string literal in the exploit binary.

Figure 5: Stage 3 — FreezeVSS worker thread: register CloudFilter provider, arm oplock, release callback, freeze confirmed.

The worker thread initiates a batch oplock on a designated lock file in the sync root, then signals the release event. During this process, the callback, which retains control over MsMpEng, invokes the CfExecute function using a placeholder for the lock file. The cldflt.sys component then handles the CfExecute call, accesses the lock file, and breaks the oplock, allowing MsMpEng to continue its operations. The entire cycle sequence occurs within a single CfExecute round-trip, allowing the exploit to perform its Stage 4 | Stage 6 operations without being hindered by Defender.

Figure 6: Stage 3 — CloudFilter callback body: identify MsMpEng as the calling process, then signal the worker thread to arm the release oplock.

MsMpEng.exe operates as a Protected Process Light (PPL) with PsProtectedSignerAntimalware protection, preventing any user-mode observers from attaching debuggers or inspecting its threads. Although Task Manager displays the process as “Running,” it can be misleading, as its main scan thread may be halted within cldflt.sys, and per-thread wait states are not visible to users with limited privileges. While PPL protects the process, exploits can weaponize it. The key action in this context is performed by a single SetEvent instruction, which releases the callback, as illustrated in detail in Figure 7.

Figure 7: Stage 3 — SetEvent pivot instruction (pink) and freeze-confirmation string (blue).

Microsoft has identified Defender Antimalware Platform version 4.18.26030.3011 as the threshold for addressing CVE-2026-33825. Endpoints that operate on this version or any later version are safeguarded against the vulnerable Defender path exploited by BlueHammer, effectively preventing access to Stage 4 of the attack.

Stage 4 — Staging Fake Definition Files

In Stage 4 of the exploit, the attacker prepares update files under their control by creating an NT object manager path structured as \Sessions\<N>\BaseNamedObjects\<GUID>. This path is established using the NtCreateDirectoryObjectEx function. Within this directory, a symbolic link named WDUpdateDirectory is created, pointing to a temporary filesystem location where in-memory update files from Stage 1 are stored. This approach is crucial because, in Stage 6, the attacker will replace the symbolic link without being detected after the Defender has accessed it.

The staged update files are designed to be byte-identical to Microsoft’s original signed versions, except for mpasbase.vdm, which is replaced with a malicious version. The remaining files retain their valid signatures, ensuring that Defender’s signature validation checks continue to succeed. It is important to note that these update files differ from the foo.exe decoy used in Stage 3, which was intended to entice MsMpEng into a CloudFilter callback that would freeze it. Instead, the focus here lies on the genuine signature-update files that Defender will eventually utilize.

Figure 8: Stage 4 — per-session object-manager directory + WDUpdateDirectory symlink setup.

Stage 5 — RPC to Defender’s Update Engine

In Stage 5 of the exploit process, the malicious update files are delivered to Windows Defender via its local update engine through an RPC interface. This interface, specifically the MpAmDefinitionUpdateAPI, is typically used for legitimate Defender signature updates and is managed by MsMpEng.exe with assistance from MpSvc.dll.

The exploit creates a worker thread, WDCallerThread that binds to the RPC interface using a specific UUID over the ncalrpc transport. It targets the endpoint designated as IMpService77BDAF73-B396-481F-9042-AD358843EC24 and invokes procedure 42, called ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature. In the compiled exploit binary, the corresponding MIDL-generated stub for this procedure has been streamlined, with the pseudocode reflecting a direct call to the core function.

Notably, the argument provided to this procedure is not a typical filesystem path; instead, it is formatted as an NT object-manager path that leads to a staging directory set up by Stage 4 of the exploit. This path can be represented as \\?\GLOBALROOT\Sessions\<N>\BaseNamedObjects\<GUID>\WDUpdateDirectory. When Defender processes these files, it successfully validates their signatures except for the manipulated mpasbase.vdm, which is disguised as a genuine Microsoft file.

As Defender creates a new SYSTEM-owned copy of the files in a subdirectory of C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Definition Updates\, the exploit actively monitors this directory using the ReadDirectoryChangesW function. It captures the name of the new subdirectory as soon as Defender completes its copy operation, allowing the exploit to proceed with its objectives.

Figure 9: Stage 5 — WDCallerThread: MpAmDefinitionUpdateAPI RPC binding and inlined Proc42 dispatch.

Stage 6 — Oplock-Timed Symlink Race

Stage 6 represents an advancement from Stage 5 by transforming the arbitrary file write as SYSTEM into a targeted file read. Specifically, it focuses on accessing the SAM registry hive from the VSS shadow copy created in Stage 2. Following Stage 5, Windows Defender creates a new directory for signature updates and populates it with SYSTEM-owned versions of the staged files. Prior to loading these new signatures, Defender reopens the mpasbase.vdm file from the WDUpdateDirectory to verify its contents. This second opening is critical, as it becomes the target of a race condition.

In this setup, a batch oplock is placed on the current mpasbase.vdm located in the exploit’s staging directory. The file is accessed with the FILE_DELETE_ON_CLOSE option via NtCreateFile, causing it to disappear immediately upon closing the handle, leaving no forensic trace. Subsequently, DeviceIoControl activates the batch oplock using FSCTL 0x90008, the same control code utilized in Stage 2. The process then leverages GetOverlappedResult to block until Defender’s second opening of the file interrupts the oplock.

Figure 10: Stage 6 setup — open mpasbase.vdm, arm batch oplock, wait for Defender to break it.

When an oplock is broken, Defender’s I/O operation is temporarily halted during the open process. The kernel intervenes by breaking the oplock and waits for the current handle holder to close before allowing Defender’s operation to continue. This situation creates a brief opportunity, typically lasting only a few hundred microseconds, for the exploit to execute a swap of the symbolic link.

During this narrow time frame, the exploit closes the existing WDUpdateDirectory symlink handle. It then creates a new symlink that points to the object-manager directory itself and introduces a new mpasbase.vdm symbolic link within that directory. This link directs to the SAM file located in the Windows System32 directory on the Stage 2 shadow copy.

Once the CloseHandle(FileHandle) function is called, it releases the paused state of Defender’s open process. At this point, Defender accesses the SAM hive using its SYSTEM token through the newly swapped symlink chain. Since Defender’s operation runs within a transaction established by the exploit, the exploit can call CreateFileTransacted with the same transaction handle to open the same file. Both handles recognize the SAM hive that Defender just accessed as SYSTEM, allowing the exploit’s handle to navigate the leaked SAM handle as Stage 7 progresses.

Figure 11: Stage 6 race — swap WDUpdateDirectory symlink, plant mpasbase.vdm → SAM, release Defender.

Stage 7 — SAM Parse to SYSTEM Shell

The final stage of the exploit, Stage 7, serves as the culmination of the previous stages, granting access to a crucial artifact: a leaked handle that allows access to the System’s SAM registry hive on a volume shadow copy (VSS). This process circumvents the standard registry API, which typically requires a hive to be mounted under HKLM or HKCU. Instead, the exploit relies on the offline registry API in offreg.dll, specifically the OROpenHiveByHandle function, to interact with the hive directly from its file bytes.

Furthermore, the Security Accounts Manager (SAM) encrypts each account’s NT hash using a unique per-machine syskey. This syskey is derived from a 16-byte value known as the LSA bootkey, which is distributed across four specific registry subkey class names located under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa. Accessing these class names requires using RegQueryInfoKey, as they are not visible via standard registry queries. A function called GetLSASecretKey navigates through these four subkeys, retrieves their class names, decodes them from hexadecimal, and applies a specific permutation to reconstruct the 16-byte bootkey.

Figure 12: Stage 7 — GetLSASecretKey: read hidden bootkey chunks from four LSA subkey class names.

The process begins with the function UnprotectPasswordEncryptionKey, which extracts the encrypted syskey blob from SAM\Domains\Account\F using the Windows CryptoAPI. This involves acquiring the “Microsoft Enhanced RSA and AES Cryptographic Provider” to import a DES-derived intermediate key and then performing a 32-byte AES-CBC decryption. This method is standard for Windows 10 and 11 and is designed to exploit the encryption chain associated with these systems while avoiding older versions that only used DES for syskeys. Once the syskey is obtained, the exploit accesses the SAM database at SAM\Domains\Account\Users\<RID>, parsing its entries to retrieve the encrypted NT hashes for each user. The function UnprotectNTHash then decrypts these hashes using the recovered syskey and the account’s RID as a salt. During testing, the administrator account with a RID of 1001 revealed a plaintext NT hash of 8846f7eaee8fb117ad06bdd830b7586c and the corresponding MD4 hash for the password “password.”

The next phase, referred to as the “swap,” occurs in two steps. The function CalculateNTLMHash is called with the plaintext password “$PWNed666!!!WDFAIL,” resulting in an MD4 hash to replace the existing NT hash. During the execution of the CalculateNTLMHash function, the RCX register directly references a specific set of plaintext bytes. These bytes are represented as a string that also appears as a literal in the binary .rdata section. This string stands out as a significant indicator of compromise (IoC) within the entire binary.

Figure 13: Stage 7 — x64dbg at CalculateNTLMHash entry: RCX points at the plaintext bytes of “$PWNed666!!!WDFAIL” as the exploit computes its new NT hash.

When changing a user password, the ChangeUserPassword function is invoked with specific parameters: the target account name in RCX, the decrypted old NT hash in RDX, and the newly generated NT hash. At the entry point of this function, the account name “admin” is stored in RCX, while R12 holds the decrypted old NT hash from the Security Account Manager (SAM). This hash is displayed in hex format, specifically “8846f7eaee8fb117ad06bdd830b7586c.”

Within ChangeUserPassword, the SamiChangePasswordUser function is invoked, replacing the admin account’s stored NT hash. A noteworthy aspect of this process is that SamiChangePasswordUser requires the old NT hash for authorization, rather than the plaintext password. As the exploit has already obtained the necessary old hash from the SAM decryption, it meets the authorization criteria.

However, it’s important to note that simply extracting the SAM does not grant elevated permissions, as you cannot use a raw NT hash to log on. Additionally, performing a password reset typically requires administrative rights. It is only when these two actions are executed together, in the specified order, that a local admin’s cached hash can be transformed into a functional password of the exploit’s choosing.

Figure 14: Stage 7 — x64dbg at ChangeUserPassword entry: RCX = L”admin”, R12 dump shows the decrypted old NTLM hash “8846f7ea…” about to be swapped via SAMR.

After the admin password is reset, the exploit uses the new credentials to log in as an administrator. It then retrieves the UAC-elevated linked token using the GetTokenInformation(TokenLinkedToken) function and impersonates the admin. With administrative authority now established, the exploit accesses the Service Control Manager and creates a temporary service. This service is assigned a random GUID name and has its ImagePath linked to the exploit’s own binary, allowing it to start successfully. The Service Control Manager (SCM) defaults to launching the service as LocalSystem.

When the service initiates, the exploit’s primary function (wmain) executes a second time. This new instance identifies itself as running as LocalSystem and shifts its approach to relocate its SYSTEM token from Session 0 to the caller’s interactive session. To facilitate this transition, it performs four consecutive SetPrivilege calls to enable the necessary privileges, including SeTcbPrivilege (needed by SetTokenInformation for cross-session operations), SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege (needed by CreateProcessAsUser), SeImpersonatePrivilege, and SeDebugPrivilege. Following these preparations, DuplicateTokenEx is used to create a new primary token, which is then redirected to the user’s session using SetTokenInformation with the TokenSessionId. Finally, the exploit successfully launches conhost.exe within that interactive session using CreateProcessAsUser.

Figure 15: Stage 7 — SYSTEM-to-user-session pivot: SetPrivilege chain + DuplicateTokenEx + SetTokenInformation(TokenSessionId).

In a security exploit scenario, two instances of the conhost.exe process appear on the desktop as the attack unfolds. One process runs under the NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM account, originating from the SYSTEM-side component of the exploit, while the other runs under the compromised administrator’s account, initiated by the original process via CreateProcessWithLogonW using the altered admin credentials.

As the exploit progresses, it restores the administrator’s original NT hash to keep the account intact. However, if the exploit’s process is terminated between the reset and the restoration phases, the administrator may inadvertently be left with a residual password: $PWNed666!!!WDFAIL. This showcases the potential risk of a vulnerability on a live host, highlighting the importance of robust security measures to prevent such exploits.

Figure 16: Stage 7 payoff — SYSTEM shell (left) and admin shell (right) spawned by the FunnyApp.exe process visible in the x64dbg title bar (PID 8308).

Beyond the Shell — Turning SYSTEM into Domain Admin

In Stage 7 of the exploit process, the attacker gains an interactive shell running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, indicating a successful local privilege escalation on the isolated exploit-analysis host. This access is significant because, within an enterprise domain, the SYSTEM account can reveal the credentials of users who have logged in to the compromised workstation. In our lab setup, we used the SYSTEM shell to retrieve sensitive data from LSASS with Mimikatz. Ultimately, this led to the discovery of the domain credentials for the CITRIX\administrator account. It’s important to note that while BlueHammer did not create these credentials, it provided the necessary SYSTEM access to extract the credential information already residing on the compromised system.

In our process, we utilized the recovered NTLM hash with the sekurlsa::pth module of Mimikatz. This allowed us to create a process that included a domain administrator’s logon session, eliminating the need for the plaintext password. Subsequently, we authenticated the domain controller using the NTLM hash through PsExec.

Figure 18: mimikatz sekurlsa::pth module spawning a new process under a spoofed domain-administrator logon session using the captured NTLM hash.

In the pass-the-hash process conducted on Node01, the local host machine, we used PsExec to connect to the domain controller, dc60. During this process, the source shell was identified as NODE01\administrator, while the command shell on the remote dc60 operated under the CITRIX\administrator account. This setup allowed us to access protected system locations, initiate services, and extract the NTDS.dit file, successfully demonstrating full control as a domain administrator.

The analysis of the remote whoami command revealed that the command shell on the dc60 workstation was operating under the CITRIX\administrator account. This finding was further validated by accessing sensitive system locations, initiating services, and extracting the NTDS.dit file. At this stage, it was clear that the security breach extended beyond a single workstation; the attacker had gained control of the domain’s built-in Administrator account, granting them access to various credentials and administrative capabilities throughout the domain.

Figure 19: Pass-the-hash session moving from NODE01\administrator to a remote command shell on domain controller dc60 as CITRIX\administrator.

The outlined sequence illustrates the complete attack path that the exploit aims to uncover. It began with a foothold gained by a standard user, followed by successful exploitation of BlueHammer, elevation to local SYSTEM privileges, and extraction of cached domain administrator credentials. The attacker then utilized pass-the-hash authentication to gain access to the domain controller, ultimately executing commands as CITRIX\administrator. Key Takeaways

Teams are remediating more than ever, but exposure from the vulnerabilities that matter is still rising faster than they can keep up with.

October is here, bringing a chill in the air, spooky decorations, and, fittingly, Cybersecurity Awareness Month. It’s a timely reminder for security leaders to revisit and strengthen their strategy. The past 12 months alone show how cyber threats are getting smarter and faster.

There’s a haunting paradox that should be top of mind. Security teams are doing more vulnerability remediation than ever before. They’re patching faster, scanning deeper, and closing more tickets than any team in history, yet attackers exploit systems at an alarming rate, faster than ever before.

Fortunately, with the right cyber risk management plan, security teams can navigate the dark landscape of AI-driven attackers. But before we talk about defense, let’s outline a few of attackers’ tricks.

The Threat Landscape Is Accelerating

Ransomware is one of the leading cyber threats, rising in both frequency and cost. It now factors into 48% of breaches, up from 44% from the previous year, and attacks are projected to occur every two seconds by 2031. If that projection holds, it will put severe pressure on already strained security teams.

AI is escalating the problem rather than easing it. AI-generated attacks have increased 56% between March 2025 and February 2026, adding $1 million in cost per breach to the baseline cost. More attacks are coming, and those powered by AI make each breach more expensive to address.

The increased frequency and sophistication combined result in a spine-chilling number: mean time to exploitation is now measured at -7 days. Which means, on average, weaponization arrives a week before defenders have anything to deploy. Mean time to remediate, by comparison, sits at +30 days. The attacker’s clock starts before defenders have anything to deploy, so the defenders are already behind before their own 30-day countdown even begins. And there’s a scary price attached.

The Financial Reality

Every hour a breach remains active costs organizations roughly $1,100 in operational disruption, lost productivity, and incident response overhead, turning every minute into a running invoice. Globally, a breach averages about $5 million per incident, up 12% from last year.

The U.S. is projected to have the highest breach cost at about $11.5 million – more than twice the global average. The Middle East, Benelux, and Germany follow, with all four regions experiencing higher breach costs than the global average.

With costs escalating like this, the expectation would be that a growing volume of patching work is buying that cost down. The data says otherwise.

The Remediation Paradox

Research by the Qualys Threat Research Unit found that while the effort to address vulnerabilities went up, exposure still rose alongside it. According to the research, effort was allocated by volume and severity score instead of by evidence of what attackers were using. As a result, enterprises did far more work and ended up further behind. Closures rose from 73 million in 2022 to 473 million in 2025, a 6x increase in output, while the share of critical vulnerabilities still open at day seven rose from 56% to 63%. More effort produced less coverage where it counted.

The reason traces back to how that effort gets allocated in the first place. Less than 1% of vulnerabilities are actively exploited, which means a program built around volume and severity score spends the majority of its effort on vulnerabilities attackers were never going to use. The 6x increase didn’t close the gap since most of that work was never aimed at the 1% that mattered.

This misalignment proves detrimental for the vulnerabilities that do get weaponized. Across the most critical, actively exploited vulnerabilities over the past four years, manual remediation processes failed to keep pace with attackers 88% of the time, and half were weaponized before a patch existed. Teams were doing the work. They just weren’t always working on the right thing, at the right time.

The light in the dark here is that there are organizations winning this race. 15% of organizations that operationalized their remediation pipeline patched before the vulnerability was even added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list. This is proof that the gap isn’t fixed in place. It closes when the model changes.

As risk accelerates, the organizations that shift away from a ‘fix everything’ mindset to disciplined, continuous, business-impact-based prioritization will be prepared for the unknown. The focus should be on automated, intelligence-driven remediation that assesses risk in real time rather than adding people to a process.

The Path Forward

So what does this shift look like? It starts with context, not more volume. Remediation becomes contextual rather than sequential. Most friction between IT and security doesn’t start with the vulnerability itself. It starts when a ticket arrives without ownership data, gets validated whether or not action is warranted, and then gets reassigned before anything is fixed.

When asset context and risk intelligence route tasks before a ticket is even created, that upstream friction disappears. MTTR drops 30% and response times improve 40%. That’s what happens when decisions about what really matters get made before the backlog forms, instead of getting caught in debates once issues arise.

In a digital age where attacks are happening faster than teams can keep up, the teams still haunted by their own remediation metrics are the ones still asking the old questions: how many vulnerabilities can we close? What’s the CVSS score? How long before we remediate? The organizations that are getting safer are asking a different set of questions: Is this actively being exploited? What’s the evidence? Which assets are at risk? What can we automate?

As we recognize Cybersecurity Awareness Month, it’s crucial to remember that diligence is non-negotiable; the real key lies in prioritizing the vulnerabilities that wield the greatest impact.

Vulnerabilities are now discovered faster than enterprises can remediate them. Patch automation has been around for years, but vulnerability backlogs are still growing. Patch automation has existed for years. Yet in most enterprises, automated remediation jobs still wait in line behind change approvals and maintenance windows while critical exposures stay open.

The reason is that risk cuts both ways. Leave a vulnerability unpatched, and you invite exploitation. Push a faulty update, and you risk failed installs, rollbacks, or outages. Without evidence of how a change will behave, Security and IT teams default to caution, and the backlog grows.

Patch automation was never the blocker. Confidence is.

Today, we’re closing this gap with TruRisk Eliminate 2.0, the Autonomous RemOps platform. Powered by TruConfidence, its AI-powered Remediation and Orchestration Intelligence engine, and Agent Sara, Qualys’ autonomous AI agent for risk remediation, TruRisk Eliminate determines the right remediation action and executes it across your entire attack surface while keeping operations resilient.

The Confidence Gap: Why the Remediation Backlog Keeps Growing

AI-powered discovery is finding vulnerabilities faster than ticket-driven remediation can close them. Patch Tuesday recently hit 974 CVEs in a single month, on a process built for about 100. Attackers are taking advantage. The Verizon 2026 DBIR found that 31% of breaches began with the exploitation of vulnerabilities, up from 20%, making it the top initial access vector.

Remediation has not kept pace. The same report shows the median time to remediate a known exploited vulnerability (KEV) rose from 32 to 43 days, and only 26% of KEVs are fully remediated. Qualys research shows the same widening gap between the speed of threats and the speed of remediation.

The ability to automate is not the constraint. Qualys customers already automate remediation at scale: automated patch deployments rose 81% between the first and second quarters of 2026. They can because Qualys gives them the evidence to trust each change, from which exposures matter to how reliably a patch will deploy. What stalls machine-speed remediation is the lack of evidence needed to confidently move beyond manual, human-led remediation workflows. Without that, automated or autonomous remediation stalls.

Before letting autonomous remediation run, Security and IT teams need answers to these questions:

What must be fixed? Only 1% of vulnerabilities are exploited in the wild. Teams need to fix the validated exposures first, then tackle the long tail.

Does it need a patch? Not every exposure needs one. A mitigation, an uninstall or an existing security control can close it faster, with less disruption.

If it needs a patch, will it work and can it be automated? Teams need to predict whether a patch is safe to deploy and will not cause any business disruption, then roll it out progressively.

How do we control the rollout? Teams need to deploy changes progressively: zero-touch automation for high-reliability patches on low-impact applications, and ring-based deployment for everything else.

Did the environment stay healthy? Teams need ensure that risk was eliminated to maintain operational resiliency.

Answer these four questions with evidence, and remediation can run at machine speed without putting business continuity at risk.

How it Fits in the Autonomous RemOps Cycle

Closing that gap takes more than a better patch tool. It takes a new operating model for remediation: Autonomous RemOps.

Traditional patch tools push what is in the catalog and stop at “deployed.” Autonomous RemOps replaces that ticket-driven process with a continuous, evidence-based Decide → Execute → Prove. It determines what to fix, executes the appropriate remediation path across the entire attack surface, and demonstrates that the business remained resilient.

TruRisk Eliminate 2.0 runs that cycle in five steps. First, Qualys ETM and Agent Val validate what must be fixed. Second, TruConfirm credits the controls already in place. TruConfidence powers the final three steps, where autonomy carries the most operational risk: choosing the remediation path, controlling the rollout, and proving that it held.

Meet TruConfidence: Remediation Intelligence You Can Trust

TruConfidence is the remediation and orchestration intelligence layer behind TruRisk Eliminate. For every exposure, it answers one question: what is the safest and most effective way to eliminate this risk? Agent Sara puts that answer to work through waves. Together, they cover the full remediation lifecycle before, during, and after every deployment.

TruConfidence Before the Deployment

Once Qualys ETM and Agent Val have validated which exposures are exploitable and TruConfirm has credited the controls already in place, TruConfidence determines the right remediation path for each exposure.

Then you can determine whether a patch is needed at all. Patchless Remediation closes exposures by mitigating, uninstalling unused software, running a custom script or isolating the host. Third-Party Mitigation Intelligence extends those options through the tools teams already run, such as Zscaler and CrowdStrike.

When a patch is the right remediation action, the AI-Powered Patch Reliability Scoring predicts whether the patch is safe to deploy before it runs, drawing on global telemetry and Qualys customer deployments.

TruConfidence During the Rollout

Agent Sara efficiently implements TruConfidence’s decisions, eliminating ticket queues. She prioritizes eliminating the exploited 1% first and then automatically addresses the remaining vulnerabilities.

She organizes the backlog into remediation waves; each matched to its level of risk. You define the waves to fit your environment, and Agent Sara runs them.

A typical setup might look like this:

Easy Fixes: High-reliability patches on low-impact assets deploy zero-touch.

Connectivity-Sensitive: Changes are sequenced carefully to protect systems with critical network dependencies.

Operational Risk: Changes are held for closer review before proceeding.

Beyond Patching: Exposures are routed to the patchless path TruConfidence selected.

Every change moves through progressive rings, from Pilot to broad deployment, and is observed before it reaches the next tier. A low-reliability signal automatically pauses progression, keeping the blast radius as small as possible.

Agent Sara works within your rules, not around them, enforcing maintenance windows, asset groupings, and rollback controls, and requires human approval wherever a critical service, identity infrastructure, or production databases are involved.

TruConfidence After the Rollout

A successful install is not the finish line. Operational Resiliency continues to correlate health signals after each change, monitoring for CPU spikes, memory issues, and service impact. Stable metrics confirm the change held, while anomalies pause the rollout and trigger rollback. When a remediation fails, AI-Powered Failure Analysis explains the root cause in plain language, such as a pending reboot or a missing prerequisite, and recommends the corrective action. Every change ends with evidence, which means faster recovery and fewer war rooms.

Remediation that reaches every corner of your attack surface

TruRisk Eliminate 2.0 goes past agent-based endpoints. It extends remediation to perimeter devices, cloud and applications, so teams can deal with an exposure wherever it lives. Each asset gets the response that fits it: patch it, mitigate the risk when no patch exists yet, uninstall the vulnerable software, isolate the asset or apply a custom fix.

For assets that can’t host an agent, Eliminate works through Qualys scanners and the security and IT integrations you already have. Every exposure gets a path to remediation, not just the ones on managed endpoints.
